analysis.one_liner: Cuts power plant sulfur, nitrogen, mercury and carbon emissions and forces 30-year-old plants to meet modern standards.
analysis.headline: Backed by 121 House members from both parties, the bill was never given a hearing or vote and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to write rules cutting power plant sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides 75% below 1997 levels by 2005, cutting mercury 90%, and bringing carbon dioxide back down to 1990 levels. It would also have required power plants that have run for 30 years or more — many of them old coal plants exempt from earlier clean air rules — to finally meet the same modern standards as new plants. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants: communities breathing smog and soot, children and pregnant women exposed to mercury, and anyone affected by acid rain. The bill also allowed market-based emission trading for sulfur and nitrogen but banned trading for mercury so pollution would not stay concentrated near particular neighborhoods.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind residents and children exposed to mercury

how_it_helps.text: Required EPA regulations cutting aggregate power plant sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions by 75% from 1997 levels by January 1, 2005, pollutants that cause acid rain, smog, and fine-particle health damage.
Required a 90% cut in mercury emissions from power plants by 2005, and specifically prohibited mercury emission trading so reductions could not be concentrated away from local communities.
Required power plant carbon dioxide emissions to return to 1990 levels by 2005 — the first time Congress would have capped utilities' carbon output.

Required 'outdated powerplants' — any plant operating 30 years or more — to meet the most recent new source performance standards, closing the gap under which old plants built before modern Clean Air Act rules could keep polluting at far higher rates than new ones.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants, especially those operating aging plants, would bear the cost of deep emission cuts and retrofits. Utilities could pass a share of those compliance costs to electricity customers through rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Owners of old coal-fired power plants

drawbacks.text: The compliance deadline was tight: regulations due within two years and 75% cuts achieved by 2005, which would have forced rapid retrofits or retirements at older plants and raised electricity prices for customers, with the burden falling hardest where coal generation dominates.

The bill gave the EPA Administrator broad discretion both in allocating reductions and in requiring additional cuts beyond the stated targets, which utilities argued left compliance costs unpredictable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains — large cuts in soot, smog, acid rain, mercury, and the first-ever power plant carbon cap — were substantial and well documented as the kinds of reductions later achieved by separate rules over a longer period. The real cost was compliance spending at coal plants, part of which would show up in electric bills. A genuine weakness was the compressed five-year timeline; the bill's own equity language and flexibility for trading mechanisms softened but did not eliminate that.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Commerce Committee and its Health and Environment subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and was never brought to a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Clean Smokestacks Act on September 21, 1999, with 15 original cosponsors from both parties.
It attracted 121 cosponsors in total — 108 Democrats, 12 Republicans, and 1 Independent — a level of support that normally guarantees floor action in the House.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce on the day of introduction, and on October 8, 1999, to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of aging coal-fired power plants were better off: they avoided the mandated 75% cuts in sulfur and nitrogen pollution, the 90% mercury cut, and a carbon cap, and kept operating under the looser rules that applied to older plants.

for.name: Henry A. Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of 15 original cosponsors.

for.name: 12 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsor Rep. Sherwood Boehlert of New York.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a markup or reported it out of committee.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.role: House Commerce subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from October 1999 onward without any hearing or action.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 108 Democrats, 12 Republicans, and 1 Independent of 121 — but the Republican-controlled Commerce Committee never acted on the bill, so support and obstruction did not divide cleanly by party.

industries.note: The bill would have cut their sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions 75%, mercury 90%, and capped carbon dioxide at 1990 levels, while requiring plants 30 years old or more to meet modern standards. Their interest ran against the public's here: the cheaper path for them was continuing to operate old plants under grandfathered pollution rules.

Deep emission cuts and retrofits at coal plants would have reduced coal demand, since utilities facing such limits would burn less coal or switch fuels. The savings to the public came in the form of cleaner air, not cheaper power.

Retrofitting hundreds of aging power plants on a five-year deadline would have created a large market for scrubbers and other control equipment. Their interest ran alongside the public's, since their business depended on the cleanups happening.
